scope: Design and analyse sine-wave oscillators built from a frequency-selective RC network and an amplifier, using the Barkhausen criterion to fix the frequency and the minimum gain, and sizing the amplitude-stabilising element.
intuition: An oscillator is a feedback amplifier that has been talked into chasing its own tail: if the loop gain has exactly unity magnitude and zero total phase shift at one frequency, a whisper at that frequency returns to the input as an identical whisper and never dies. The RC network is the filter that picks the frequency by arranging its phase shift to pass through the required value, and the amplifier's gain must be just large enough to replace the energy the network throws away.
concept: **Barkhausen: one frequency, two conditions.** Sustained oscillation requires that the signal travelling once around the loop return with the same magnitude and the same phase. In the negative-feedback convention that is $A\beta = -1$; stated as magnitude and phase it is $|A\beta| = 1$ with a total loop phase of $0^\circ$ (equivalently $360^\circ$). The frequency of oscillation is the frequency at which the *phase* condition holds - the magnitude condition then merely fixes the gain. In practice $|A\beta|$ is designed a few percent above 1 so that noise can start the oscillation, and some nonlinear or automatic mechanism pulls the effective loop gain back to exactly 1 once the amplitude is large enough. That mechanism is not a refinement; without it the amplitude either decays to nothing or grows until the amplifier clips.

**The RC phase-shift oscillator.** The network is three (never two) RC sections, each designed to contribute $60^\circ$ of phase at the design frequency so that the network supplies the $180^\circ$ the inverting amplifier cannot. Three sections are the minimum because a single section can only approach $90^\circ$, so two sections only reach $180^\circ$ asymptotically as the frequency falls to zero, where the attenuation also falls to zero and an infinite gain would be needed. At the design frequency the exact ladder analysis gives $f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC\sqrt{6})$ and an attenuation of exactly $1/29$, so the amplifier must supply $|A| \ge 29$. Since the network inverts by $180^\circ$, an inverting amplifier is used, and its gain is set by $|A| = R_f/R_{in} \ge 29$. The frequency is set by the RC product alone, but the phase condition is what actually selects it, so any additional phase shift in the amplifier (from its own bandwidth) shifts $f_0$.

**The Wien bridge.** The Wien network is a series RC arm and a parallel RC arm forming a lead-lag divider. Its phase passes through exactly $0^\circ$ at $\omega_0 = 1/RC$, and at that frequency the divider ratio is exactly $\beta = 1/3$; away from $\omega_0$ the phase changes rapidly, which is why the Wien bridge is far more frequency-selective (and produces much less distortion) than the three-section ladder. Because the network's phase at $f_0$ is zero, a non-inverting amplifier is used, and the gain condition $1 + R_f/R_1 = 3$ means $R_f/R_1 = 2$ exactly. The tuning relationship is $f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC)$, so equal resistors and equal capacitors in the two arms give the design frequency; tuning is usually done with a ganged two-section capacitor or a two-gang resistor, since any mismatch between the series and parallel arms moves the zero-phase point off the nominal frequency.

**Amplitude stabilisation and the cost of excess gain.** If the gain is set to exactly 3 the circuit sits on the edge: any loss in the network makes $|A\beta|$ slightly less than 1 and the oscillation dies, so a designer starts with a little extra gain. But a fixed gain of, say, 3.2 makes $|A\beta| = 1.067$, and the amplitude grows exponentially until the amplifier's own clipping reduces the effective (fundamental) gain to 3. The clipped waveform has 10 to 20 percent total harmonic distortion - audible and unacceptable for a signal generator. The standard fix is a tungsten-filament lamp in the ground arm of the feedback divider: as the amplitude rises the filament heats, its resistance rises, and since $A = 1 + R_f/R_{lamp}$, the gain falls. With $R_f = 220\ \Omega$ a lamp that is $100\ \Omega$ cold gives $A = 3.2$ (start-up margin) and $115\ \Omega$ hot gives $A = 2.91$ (amplitude falling), so the circuit settles at the lamp resistance for which $A = 3$ exactly, here $110\ \Omega$. Thermistors, diode limiters and JFET-as-variable-resistor AGC circuits do the same job; the key requirement is that the control element sit in the *ground* arm, where an increase in resistance lowers the gain.

**Where the ideal formulas stop working.** Every number above assumes the network is driven by a zero-impedance source and read by an infinite impedance. Real op-amp input resistance shunts the last section of the ladder: with $R = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 10\ \mathrm{nF}$, an amplifier input resistance of $10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ halves the final shunt resistance and moves $f_0$ from $649.7\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $750.3\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (a $+15.5\%$ error) while the attenuation rises from $1/29$ to $1/39.5$, so the minimum gain becomes 40 rather than 29. The op-amp's own excess phase at high frequency pulls $f_0$ low and can kill the oscillation. Slew rate sets a ceiling on the achievable frequency for a given amplitude, and stray capacitance across the resistors shifts the Wien frequency upward. A practical oscillator therefore has its frequency trimmed on the bench, and its gain verified as greater than $1/\beta$ by a comfortable margin.

formulas.n: The phase condition sets the frequency; the magnitude condition sets the minimum gain. A loop gain slightly above 1 is used for start-up, with an amplitude-limiting mechanism to bring the effective value back to 1.
Three identical sections with equal R and C, each contributing 60 degrees at f_0. With R = 10 k-ohm and C = 10 nF this is 649.7 Hz. Forgetting the sqrt(6) gives 1591.5 Hz, a 2.45x error.
Exact for three identical sections driven by a zero-impedance source and read by an infinite impedance. Loading by the amplifier input raises it (1/39.5 with a 10 k-ohm load on a 10 k-ohm ladder).
An inverting amplifier is required because the ladder already supplies 180 degrees; its gain is R_f/R_in, so R_in = 1 k-ohm needs R_f of at least 29 k-ohm.
Equal R and equal C in the series and parallel arms. R = 1.6 k-ohm with C = 0.1 micro-F gives 994.7 Hz. Any mismatch between the arms moves the zero-phase frequency away from this value.
At f_0 only, where the lead-lag network's phase is exactly zero. Away from f_0 the magnitude falls and the phase swings rapidly, which is what makes the Wien bridge selective.
Non-inverting amplifier, so the network's zero phase is preserved. A ratio below 2 gives a gain below 3 and the oscillation dies; a ratio above 2 requires amplitude limiting to prevent clipping.

The lamp goes in the GROUND arm so that rising amplitude raises its resistance and lowers the gain. R_f = 220 ohm with a lamp of 100 ohm cold gives A = 3.2; at 115 ohm hot A = 2.91; equilibrium is at 110 ohm where A = 3.

problems.prompt: An RC phase-shift oscillator uses three identical sections with $R = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 10\ \mathrm{nF}$. Find the oscillation frequency, the network attenuation at that frequency, and the feedback resistor needed for an inverting amplifier with $R_{in} = 1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$. State the resulting loop gain if $R_f = 33\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ is used.
steps: At $f_0$ each section contributes $60^\circ$, giving the $180^\circ$ the network must add to the amplifier's own $180^\circ$ inversion.
The exact ladder analysis gives $\beta = 1/29 = 0.03448$ at $f_0$, so the minimum gain is $|A| \ge 29$.
For an inverting amplifier $|A| = R_f/R_{in}$, so $R_f \ge 29\times1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega = 29\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$.

Choosing the standard value $R_f = 33\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ gives $|A| = 33$ and a loop gain $|A\beta| = 33/29 = 1.138$, a $13.8\%$ start-up margin that will clip unless an amplitude limiter is included.
Check the design frequency against the period: $T_0 = 1/649.7 = 1.539\ \mathrm{ms}$, and $2\pi RC\sqrt{6} = 1.5391\ \mathrm{ms}$, consistent.
problems.ans: $f_0 = 649.7\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $\beta = 1/29$, $R_f \ge 29\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ for $|A| \ge 29$; with $R_f = 33\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ the loop gain is 1.138
problems.trap: Using $f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC)$ for the ladder. That is the Wien-bridge formula; here it gives $1591.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$, which is $\sqrt{6} = 2.45$ times too high. The $\sqrt{6}$ appears because the three sections must combine to 180 degrees, not because of any single-section corner.

steps: `1 ÷ (2π × 10E3 × 10E-9 × √6)` → $f_0$ = **649.7** Hz; the `√6` is the whole difference from the Wien formula.
Minimum `29 × 1` → $R_f \ge$ **29** k$\Omega$; with the 33 k$\Omega$ standard value, `33 ÷ 29` → $\lvert A\beta \rvert$ = **1.138**, a 13.8 % start-up margin.

problems.prompt: An RC phase-shift oscillator must run at $f_0 = 2\ \mathrm{kHz}$ using $C = 10\ \mathrm{nF}$ and an inverting amplifier with $R_{in} = 1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$. Find the required $R$, the nearest standard value, the resulting frequency, and the minimum $R_f$.
steps: Solve the frequency relation for R: $R = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f_0C\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(2000)(10^{-8})(2.4495)}$.
$R = 1/(3.0782\times10^{-4}) = 3248.7\ \Omega$, so the nearest standard value is $3.3\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$.
Resulting frequency: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(3300)(10^{-8})(2.4495)} = \dfrac{1}{5.0789\times10^{-4}} = 1968.9\ \mathrm{Hz}$ - about $1.6\%$ low.
Minimum gain is still 29, so $R_f \ge 29\times1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega = 29\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$; the standard 33 k-ohm gives $|A\beta| = 1.138$.
If the exact 2 kHz matters, shunt the 3.3 k-ohm with a trimmer or use $R = 3.24\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ from a 1 percent series, since the frequency is inversely proportional to R.
problems.trap: Applying the Wien-bridge formula $R = 1/(2\pi f_0C)$ and getting $7.96\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ - a resistor $2.45$ times too large, which puts the oscillator at 818 Hz instead of 2 kHz. The $\sqrt{6}$ belongs in the denominator of the phase-shift design equation and nowhere else.

steps: `1 ÷ (2π × 2000 × 10E-9 × √6)` → $R$ = **3249** $\Omega$, so use the **3.3** k$\Omega$ standard value.
`29 × 1` → $R_f \ge$ **29** k$\Omega$; the standard 33 k$\Omega$ gives `33 ÷ 29` → **1.138**.

problems.prompt: A Wien-bridge oscillator uses $R = 1.6\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 0.1\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ in both arms of the frequency-selective network. Find the oscillation frequency, the network's feedback factor at that frequency, and the resistor ratio for the non-inverting amplifier. If the lower resistor is $R_1 = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, find $R_f$.
steps: Verify the zero-phase condition: at $\omega_0 = 1/RC$ the series arm is $R(1 - j)$ and the parallel arm is $R(1 - j)/2$, so $\beta = \dfrac{R(1-j)/2}{R(1-j) + R(1-j)/2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ with zero phase.
Gain condition: the amplifier must supply exactly the reciprocal, $A = 3$, and the network being non-inverting at $f_0$ means a non-inverting amplifier configuration is used.
For $A = 1 + R_f/R_1 = 3$: $R_f/R_1 = 2$, so $R_f = 2(10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega) = 20\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$.
Loop gain check: $|A\beta| = 3\times(1/3) = 1$, exactly the Barkhausen magnitude condition at the frequency where the loop phase is $0^\circ$.

Note the marginality: exactly $A = 3$ leaves no start-up margin, so in practice $R_f$ is set a few percent high (20.5 k-ohm gives $A = 3.05$) and a lamp or limiter is used to bring the steady-state loop gain back to 1.
problems.trap: Writing $R_1/R_f = 2$ instead of $R_f/R_1 = 2$. The gain is $1 + R_f/R_1$, so the feedback resistor must be twice the ground resistor; inverting the ratio gives $A = 1.5$, the loop gain becomes $0.5$ and the circuit never oscillates. Setting $R_f = R_1 = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ ($A = 2$) fails the same way.

steps: Loop check: `3 × (1 ÷ 3)` → **1.000**, the Barkhausen magnitude at the zero-phase frequency.

problems.prompt: A Wien-bridge oscillator uses a tungsten lamp of cold resistance $100\ \Omega$ as the ground-arm element with $R_f = 220\ \Omega$. Find the gain with the lamp cold and with the lamp at $115\ \Omega$ hot, and the lamp resistance at which the amplitude settles. State what happens if the lamp is replaced by a fixed $100\ \Omega$ resistor.
steps: A loop gain of 1.067 exceeds 1, so the oscillation amplitude grows from noise - the required start-up margin.
Hot lamp: $A = 1 + 220/115 = 1 + 1.913 = 2.913$, so $|A\beta| = 0.971$ and the amplitude now decays.
The amplitude therefore settles at the lamp resistance where $A = 3$ exactly: $1 + 220/R_{lamp} = 3$ gives $R_{lamp} = 220/2 = 110\ \Omega$, between the cold and hot values.
With a fixed $100\ \Omega$ resistor the gain stays at 3.20 and $|A\beta| = 1.067$ forever, so the output grows until the amplifier clips at its supply rails.

The clipped output is a flat-topped wave whose fundamental amplitude is about $4V_{sat}/\pi$ for a hard-limited sine - for $\pm12\ \mathrm{V}$ rails that is $15.3\ \mathrm{V}$ peak, with roughly 10 to 20 percent total harmonic distortion.

Note also the thermal time constant: the lamp must be slow compared with one cycle but fast enough to track envelope changes, which is why a small filament lamp works and a thermistor needs careful selection.
problems.ans: $A = 3.20$ cold and $2.913$ hot, settling at $R_{lamp} = 110\ \Omega$; with a fixed $100\ \Omega$ resistor the loop gain stays at 1.067 and the output clips with 10-20% THD
problems.trap: Placing the amplitude-control element in the feedback arm. With the lamp at $R_f$, a rising amplitude raises the lamp resistance and raises the gain $1 + R_f/R_1$, so the control acts with the WRONG sign: the amplitude latches to the supply rail instead of stabilising. The lamp (or thermistor, or JFET) belongs in the ground arm, where more resistance means less gain.

steps: `1 + 220 ÷ 100` → $A$ = **3.20** cold, so $\lvert A\beta \rvert$ = **1.067**, the start-up margin.
`1 + 220 ÷ 115` → $A$ = **2.913**, so $\lvert A\beta \rvert$ = **0.971** and the amplitude decays.
Equilibrium: `220 ÷ (3 − 1)` → $R_{lamp}$ = **110** $\Omega$, between the cold and hot values.

problems.prompt: A student builds a phase-shift oscillator with only two RC sections and an inverting amplifier. Show that the network cannot produce $180^\circ$ at any finite frequency, and state the consequence. Then compute the frequency and gain the three-section version needs if $R = 4.7\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 22\ \mathrm{nF}$.
steps: For two sections with $RC = 1$ and $s = j\omega RC$, nodal analysis gives $\beta = \dfrac{s^{2}}{s^{2} + 3s + 1}$.
Substituting $s = jx$: $\beta = \dfrac{-x^{2}}{(1 - x^{2}) + j3x}$.
A $180^\circ$ network phase requires $\beta$ to be real and negative, so the denominator must be purely real: $3x = 0$, hence $x = \omega RC = 0$.

At $x = 0$ the numerator is also zero, so $\beta = 0$: the two-section network reaches $180^\circ$ only at DC with zero output, and the required gain is $1/\beta \to \infty$. Two sections can never work.
Three sections remove the problem: $\beta = \dfrac{s^{3}}{s^{3} + 6s^{2} + 5s + 1}$ and the $180^\circ$ condition $\mathrm{Re} = 0$ gives $x^{2} = 1/6$, i.e. $x = 1/\sqrt{6}$.

The magnitude at that frequency is $|\beta| = 1/29$, so the inverting amplifier needs $|A| \ge 29$; with $R_{in} = 2.2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, $R_f \ge 63.8\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, satisfied by the standard 68 k-ohm.
problems.ans: Two sections give $\beta = 0$ as the only $180^\circ$ solution, so at least three are required; with three sections at $R = 4.7\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 22\ \mathrm{nF}$, $f_0 = 628.4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $|A| \ge 29$
problems.trap: Assuming each RC section contributes a clean $90^\circ$ and concluding that two sections give $180^\circ$. Each section only approaches $90^\circ$ asymptotically, and the exact two-section ladder puts the $180^\circ$ point at zero frequency where the attenuation is total. Building a two-section oscillator yields a circuit that either does not oscillate or oscillates at a frequency set by stray capacitance and op-amp phase shift rather than by the RC values.

steps: Three sections still give $\beta$ = 1/29, so `29 × 2.2` → $R_f \ge$ **63.8** k$\Omega$, met by the standard 68 k$\Omega$.

traps: **Using $f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC)$ for the three-section ladder.** The phase-shift design equation is $1/(2\pi RC\sqrt{6})$; with $R = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 10\ \mathrm{nF}$ the wrong formula gives $1591.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$ instead of $649.7\ \mathrm{Hz}$, a $\sqrt{6} = 2.45$ times error.

**Two RC sections instead of three.** Exactly $180^\circ$ from a two-section ladder requires $\omega RC = 0$, where $\beta = 0$ and the gain must be infinite. The network must supply $180^\circ$ only because the amplifier is inverting; if the amplifier is non-inverting the network would have to supply $0^\circ$ or $360^\circ$, which needs a different (typically Wien) network.

**Designing the Wien bridge with a fixed gain of exactly 3.** $|A\beta| = 1$ exactly means the circuit sits on the knife edge: with any network loss the oscillation dies out. Yet a fixed gain of 3.2 keeps $|A\beta| = 1.067$ forever and the output clips, which for $\pm12\ \mathrm{V}$ rails means a fundamental of about $4(12)/\pi = 15.3\ \mathrm{V}$ peak with 10 to 20 percent THD. The lamp or AGC is what makes the steady-state loop gain exactly 1.

**Putting the lamp in the feedback arm.** In the ground arm the lamp gives $A = 1 + R_f/R_{lamp}$, so heating lowers the gain and the amplitude is stable. In the feedback arm $A = 1 + R_{lamp}/R_1$, so heating RAISES the gain, the AGC has the wrong sign, and the amplitude latches to the supply rail.

**Reversing the Wien gain ratio.** $R_f/R_1 = 2$ gives $A = 3$; $R_1/R_f = 2$ gives $A = 1.5$ and the loop gain is only 0.5, so the oscillator never starts. Equally, using the inverting configuration with the Wien network destroys the zero-phase property at $f_0$ and the phase condition is met at some other frequency.

**Ignoring the loading of the frequency-selective network.** The $1/29$ figure assumes a zero-impedance source and an infinite load. With $R = 10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, $C = 10\ \mathrm{nF}$ and an amplifier input resistance of $10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, the last shunt element is halved, $f_0$ moves from $649.7\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $750.3\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ($+15.5\%$) and the attenuation rises from $1/29$ to $1/39.5$, so the minimum gain becomes 40 instead of 29.
